TOXIDROMES 
 
CHOLINERGIC 
 
*Common agents: 
 
Organophosphates, Carbamates, Physostigmine,   
                                    
 
mushroom toxins 
*Clinical features:  
Salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhoea, 
vomiting, sweating, miosis, fasciculations, 
brady/tachycardia, confusion, seizures 
*Investigations:  
As per toxicology protocols, 
pseudocholinesterase levels if diagnosis in doubt 
*Specific management:  
Atropine boluses/infusion 
 
   SEE ACETYLCHOLINESTERASE INHIBITOR OVERDOSE PROTOCOL FOR FURTHER DETAILS 
SYMPATHOMIMETIC 
 
*Common agents:  
Amphetamines (“Tik”), cocaine, withdrawal states,  
                             
hypermetabolic syndromes (MH, NMS), various   
                             
illicit novel street drugs, “body packers” 
*Clinical features:  
agitation, delusions, paranoia, tachycardia,  
                             
hypertension, hyperthermia, mydriasis,  
                                  hyperreflexia, seizures  
*Investigations:  
ECG for tachydysrhythmias, monitor for  
                                rhabdomyolysis  
*Specific management:  
•
Benzodiazepines for agitation 
•
Supportive care 
•
Avoid Beta-blockers – unopposed alpha agonism 
ANTICHOLINERGIC 
 
* Common agents:   
Antihistamines, antiparkinsonians,  
atropine, antispasmodics, plant 
toxins – Devil’s trumpet,  Jimson 
weed, Nightshade 
* Clinical features:  
Delirium, tachycardia, dry/flushed 
skin, dilated pupils, hyperthermia, 
myoclonus, urinary retention, 
seizures, decreased bowel sounds 
* Investigations:  
ECG – monitor for 
tachydysrhythmias 
* Specific management:  
 
•
Benzodiazepines for agitation 
•
Consider activated charcoal,  
•
Consider physostigmine (expert consultation) 
SEDATIVE-HYPNOTIC 
 
* Common agents:  Opioids, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, Nyaope & 
other opioid based illicit substances 
* Clinical features:  
sedation, coma, respiratory and cardiovascular 
depression, miosis/mydriasis 
* Investigations:  
Clinical dx, consider urine drugs of abuse screen 
* Specific management:  
•
Opioids: Consider Naloxone 0.04 – 2 mg IV boluses 
•
Benzos: Avoid Flumazenil – can precipitate withdrawal/seizures 
 
MAINSTAY OF TREATMENT FOR ALL SEDATIVE-HYPNOTICS IS VENTILATORY AND 
CARDIOVASCULAR SUPPORT 
Dr J du Plessis / Dr R Gihwala  CMJAH Emergency Department June 2020 
Contents

 
TRIAGE 
• From the French word “trier”, literally means: “to sort”. 
• The aim is to bring “the greatest good to the greatest number of people”. 
• This is achieved through prioritising limited resources to achieve the greatest possible benefit. 
• Patients are sorted with a scientific triage scale in order of urgency. 
• The end result is that the patient with the greatest need is helped first.  
CMJAH EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT  
TRIAGE PROCESS  
 
• ALL NEW PATIENTS AND ALL THOSE BROUGHT TO THE HOSPITAL BY AMBULANCE ARE TRIAGED. 
• There are 2 triage areas  
o Emergency Department (ED) Area 165 
o Area 160 24 hours - Stable walk-in and refer
